Broken Calculator

ArithmeticMental Math
Game: This calculator has most of its keys broken. Can you make every number from 1 to 15 with the keys that still work?
How to play: Press the lit keys to type a calculation, then press equals. A number you make gets ticked off above the calculator; you can find them in any order.

Numbers found: none yet

0

The crossed-out keys are broken this round. You can also type on the keyboard; Enter means equals.

Look for the math

A broken tool can still teach you something. Each round of this calculator switches off most of its keys, so getting to a number is a small puzzle in mental calculation rather than a job for a machine.

Which keys survive

Every round keeps the 0 key and chooses four different digits from 2 to 9. The 1 key never works, so to make 1 you have to build it from other digits, for example 2 / 2. One of × and ÷ works, one of + and − works, and the decimal point comes with ×. The page says only a few buttons are functional at any time, and the logic test confirms this for 2,000 generated rounds: at most 16 keys work, including the optional memory keys.

Fractions, not rounding

The calculator keeps numbers as exact fractions: 3 / 2 stays three halves and only becomes 1.5 when shown on the display. Dividing by zero gives the applet's message Bad number. A total is ticked off only when the answer is a whole number from 1 to 15; 2 / 2 counts as 1, but 3 / 2 does not.

Checking the words on the page

The fifteen numbers may be found in any order: the logic test tries all 720 orders of 1 to 6 and the list comes out the same each time. When all fifteen are found, the list ends with !. The essay also repeats two stray claims: that a drop of 60% followed by a rise of 70% leaves scores 10% higher, and that two 50% chances of rain add to 100%. Neither is right. The first is 0.4 × 1.7 = 0.68, which is 32% lower; the second adds chances for different days as though they could not both happen. That is the point of percentages: the arithmetic is easy, but the meaning needs care.

Try to make 1 without a 1 key, then see how many numbers you can reach before the list ends with an exclamation mark.
